title: The Squeaky Cloud Adventure
markdown:
Eva flew modest planes the way some people folded shirts: corners true, nothing left to chance. She did not miss corporate behemoths. She missed alignment. Pretzels standing guard over chocolate. Crackers in a phalanx around pastries. If a packet shifted, a shiver went through her, as if the sky had loosened a bolt she was meant to have checked.

Mo’s workshop hummed with gizmos and the perfume of burnt solder. His fingers were dragonflies. His nerves were not. He could stare at a working device and wait for it to self-immolate from sheer personality. On the bench lay the Inflatable Comfort Cloud — promised oasis of fluffy air, presently a deflated marshmallow. If it remained a prototype, Mo feared he would too: a man of almosts, swallowed by the next unfinished thing.

Eva had just flown a cabin of monarchs. A gentleman required coffee at seventy-two degrees Fahrenheit, no more, no less. A lady required a personal cloud for shade. Eva wanted a quiet landing, lukewarm tea, and the ballet of crisps. The uncontrolled lived just past the edge of her tray table, and she preferred it stay there.

Mo clutched the sad Cloud. He needed a test or the void would keep the seed.

Zephyr Leap arrived like a rogue comet. Posters shrieked luxury for pennies. Inaugural flight within the week. No pilot, no airline, no chance for the Cloud. Eva signed from professional duty and a morbid curiosity that felt like a cabin bug. Mo shuffled aboard because a free ticket was a king’s ransom in his budget and because the Cloud would never bloom among silent prototypes.

The aircraft looked cobbled from an enthusiastic yard sale, optimism, and what appeared to be very strong duct tape. A seatbelt sign flickered in three languages, one of them invented. Eva walked the aisle once, counting rivets the way she counted crackers, and decided not to share the total with Mo.

The sky, which usually parted for Eva, declared war on sensible airflow. Gusts tugged with the malice of a child and a kite. The tin can lurched in a cosmic bathtub. A trolley tried to launch itself. The attendant, heroic, sat on it.

Then the screens flickered. Urination Opportunity: $5.99. Relieve yourself and your wallet. Atmospheric Rejuvenation Spray: $12.50, to banish the scent of economy and existential dread. A child asked if the wings were extra. The attendant smiled the smile of someone who had been briefed not to answer.

Mo puffed the Cloud. It swelled with a noise like a thousand rubber ducks squeezed by a strong toddler, then squeaked — prolonged, ear-splitting, soul-shattering, a vibration in the rivets. Eva fought an updraft that wanted them upside down and inside out. The sound was a banshee in a wind tunnel.

“Mo. Make the squeak stop.”

He fiddled buttons labelled with runes. He jiggled levers that had been coat hangers. The squeak went operatic, a wavering lament of synthetic polyester. A bead of sweat ran his temple. He almost wished himself back in the quiet workshop. The Cloud, traitor, was also rather comfortable if you ignored the soundtrack. A passenger two rows back began to conduct.

Against odds and airflow, they descended. They did not glide. They plummeted, thumped, and discovered the runway was a farmer’s field wearing a windsock and a goat with opinions. Thrill-seekers cheered as if they had paid for this specific goat. Budget travellers clutched flimsy bags and blinked at cows who had not bought tickets. The Cloud still wailed and was, as advertised, inflated, a lumpy throne for Mo’s unfortunate occupant — himself. Arrival felt like finding Atlantis with a coupon code and a receipt for peanuts.

Eva shut down what could be shut down. Mo apologised to the Cloud, which did not accept apologies. A farmer asked if this was the new bus. Eva said, in her captain voice, that it was a conversation.

The journey’s end was the beginning of the bill. Complimentary refreshments were priced to make a dragon blush. A single packet of peanuts cost more than a small island nation and came with a waiver. Water was complimentary if you counted the condensation. The Cloud’s triumphant squeak matured into a shriek that bounced off bulkhead, ear, and nerve ending, a symphony of pure annoyance. Eva’s snack reserves were gone, spent on not screaming and on one emergency pretzel she had shared with a child who had asked whether wings were extra. She had one squashed granola bar left, a forlorn relic of her packing ritual. With a sigh that carried missed connections and lost luggage, she offered it. Mo accepted, hands still trembling, and ate it in two noisy bites that almost drowned the foam. A small comfort. Shared crumbs in the face of performance art posing as an airline. He said thank you as if she had handed him a runway.

The Zephyr Leap loomed for the return, patchwork sagging with the weariness of a brief chaotic life. Someone had already written a review: two stars, five squeaks. Eva looked at Mo’s sheepish grin under the perpetual anxiety, a flicker of accomplishment in the sonic mess. Mo fidgeted with the famous Cloud and was not entirely consumed. They had faced the shriek and the impeccably packed snacks and lived. The squeak was becoming an old irritating friend who still, somehow, had a boarding pass.

Boarding again, Eva no longer required the pretzels to stand exactly so. She packed them loose, a small heresy, and survived it. The most edible victories, she was learning, arrived improvised, with a side of unexpected noise. She could fly currents, monarchs, and chaos, and almost smile when the cabin filled with that wail. Mo felt pride as foreign as a ten-dollar bill in a winter coat. The Cloud had flown. It had been tested. It was no longer only a figment of anxious imagination. He still felt the familiar tightening. It was a gentle hum of what-if, not a thunderous shout of doom. He promised the Cloud a quieter valve and did not promise the passengers the same.

As they lumbered up — the field, the goat, the farmer’s bus theory falling away — Mo sketched improvements on a napkin, brow furrowed in the old way that now had somewhere to go. A faint persistent squeak filled the cabin, familiar as recycled air. Eva glanced at him and did not reach to rearrange a single packet. She found she did not want the sound to stop. It was the soundtrack of having left the ground on purpose, duct tape, pennies, and all.
characters: Eva (a budget-airline pilot), Mo (an anxious gadget inventor)
author: StoryGen Community
